sections.html: L114, Pseudacanthicus cf. leopardus, is a loricariid collected mostly in the rio Negro basin in Brazil, particularly the rio Demini. P. leopardus was described from the Rupununi River in Guyana, so the identity of this fish remains unconfirmed. Traded as the Demini leopard cactus pleco or simply 'leopard cactus pleco', it grows to 25 cm and needs an aquarium of at least 180 x 60 cm set up to simulate a flowing river.

Species of Pseudacanthicus are also known under their popular name “cactus catfish”, for the species are very spiny and it is no good idea to catch a larger specimen with bare hands. Some species of Pseudacanthicus can reach one metre in length, but there are other species that grow up only to 25 cm. As a rule one must be aware that Pseudacanthicus become bigger than many other common aquarium fish.

Mostly collected in the rio Negro basin, Amazonas state, Brazil, and in particular the rio Demini, a northern tributary flowing into the central Negro in the municipality of Barcelos.

P. leopardus was described from the Rupununi River in Guyana and the identity of this fish thus remains unconfirmed.

One of the most popular Pseudacanthicus is L114, which originates from the middle Rio Negro basin in Brazil. This cactus cat was thought to represent the described species Pseudacanthicus leopardus for a long time. However, the real P. leopardus originates from the border region of Brazil and Guyana. There are only very few catchers of ornamental fish in that region. The fish were collected in the Takutu river that belongs to the system of the upper Rio Branco.

Standard length: 25 cm SL.

An aquarium with base dimensions of 180 × 60 cm or larger is required for long-term care (volume ~648 litres).

Not difficult to maintain under the correct conditions; it is strongly recommended to keep it in a tank designed to simulate a flowing river with a substrate of variably-sized rocks, sand, fine gravel, and some water-worn boulders.

This can be further furnished with driftwood branches, terracotta pipes, plant pots, etc., arranged to form a network of nooks, crannies, and shaded spots, thus providing broken lines of sight.

Wild specimens are likely omnivorous but with a preference for aquatic invertebrates and suchlike.

In the aquarium it does best when offered a varied diet comprising sinking dried foods, frozen Daphnia, mosquito larvae, chironomid larvae (bloodworm), and prawn/shrimp, for example, plus some fresh fruit, parboiled potato, etc.

Home-made foods using a mixture of natural ingredients bound with gelatin are very useful since they can be tailored to contain fresh vegetables, Spirulina and meatier ingredients.
Larger specimens are quarrelsome against congeners and so roomy tanks with a lot of hiding places are needed for Pseudacanthicus.
Adult males possess a broader head plus more extensive odontode development than females, particularly on the leading pectoral-fin rays and interopercular region.
Males are more robust than females (they have especially a broader and heavier head) and have more spines during breeding season.
Cave-spawner with the male responsible for brood care. Has been bred in aquaria.
There are reports of successful breeding of some species in the aquarium. The fish are typical cave brooders.

This 'species' is also traded simply as 'leopard cactus pleco'.

Etymology: Pseudacanthicus comes from the Greek ψευδής (pseudes) meaning 'false', and the generic name Acanthicus.

Compared with L114 the fish are much flatter and have a slightly different coloration.

Almost simultaneously the numbers L114 and LDA7 were given for the same fish in different magazines. Both numbers refer to the Pseudacanthicus from the middle Rio Negro. However, when the “real” Pseudacanthicus leopardus appeared in the ornamental fish trade, the number LDA7 was used for that fish from then on. Despite this being “technically” wrong, the number LDA7 as a popular name is very well established among hobbyists for Pseudacanthicus leopardus to distinguish it from the similar L114.
• Stawikowski, R., A. Werner and I. Seidel (2004). DATZ Special: L-Numbers. DATZ, 1-132
